stem: Electricity of US\$240 is owing at the year end. How is it shown?

options.content: Added to electricity expense and shown as a current liability
options.rationale: Correct: the expense belongs to this year and is still owed.

options.content: Deducted from electricity expense and shown as a current asset
options.rationale: That is the treatment of a prepayment.

options.content: Added to electricity expense and shown as a current asset
options.rationale: An amount owed is a liability, not an asset.

options.content: Shown as a current liability only, with no change to the expense
options.rationale: The expense must include the amount owing (matching).

explanation: An accrued expense increases the expense and is an other payable (current liability).

stem: Rent received includes US\$400 paid by a tenant for next year. How is the US\$400 treated?

options.content: Deducted from rent received and shown as a current liability
options.rationale: Correct: it is income in advance, owed back as a service.

options.content: Added to rent received and shown as a current asset
options.rationale: That is the treatment of income due (accrued income).

options.content: Deducted from rent received and shown as a current asset
options.rationale: Money received for next year is a liability.

options.content: Left in rent received because the cash has been received
options.rationale: Income is matched to the period it relates to, not the date of receipt.

explanation: Income received in advance reduces this year's income and is an other payable.

stem: Trade receivables are US\$12,700 before writing off an irrecoverable debt of US\$300. The allowance for irrecoverable debts is to be 5% of the remaining receivables; it was US\$470. What amount for the allowance appears in the income statement?

options.rationale: Correct: new allowance 620 less old allowance 470.
This charges the whole new allowance instead of the change.
This calculates the allowance before the write-off.
The allowance rose from 470 to 620: it is an increase.

hints: Write off the debt first, then take the percentage.

stem: The trial balance shows motor vehicles at cost US\$32,000 and provision for depreciation US\$12,800. Depreciation is 20% per annum on the reducing balance. What is the depreciation charge for the year?

options.rationale: This is 20% of cost: the straight-line answer.
This takes 20% of the provision instead of the net book value.
This is the net book value after the charge.

stem: An accrual for wages of US\$300 was **omitted** from the financial statements. What is the effect?

options.content: Profit understated by US\$300; working capital understated by US\$300
options.rationale: Leaving out an expense makes profit too high, not too low.

options.content: Profit overstated by US\$300; working capital unaffected
options.rationale: The missing other payable is a current liability, so working capital is affected.

options.content: Profit overstated by US\$300; working capital overstated by US\$300
options.rationale: Correct: the expense is too low and a current liability is missing.

options.content: Profit unaffected; current liabilities understated by US\$300
options.rationale: The wages expense is understated, so profit is affected.

explanation: Omitting the accrual understates wages (profit too high) and understates current liabilities (working capital too high).
hints: Trace both effects of the accrual.

stem: Closing inventory was **understated** by US\$700. Which figures are understated as a result?

options.content: Cost of sales and current liabilities
options.rationale: Cost of sales is overstated; liabilities are not affected.
Revenue is not affected by inventory.

options.content: Gross profit, profit for the year, current assets and closing capital
options.rationale: Correct: cost of sales is overstated, so all four are too low.

options.content: Current assets and capital only; profit is not affected at all
options.rationale: Closing inventory is deducted in cost of sales, so profit is affected.

explanation: A lower closing inventory raises cost of sales, cutting gross profit, profit and capital, and lowers current assets.
hints: Closing inventory appears in both statements.

stem: Insurance paid of US\$2,160 covers the 12 months to 31 March 2026. The year end is 31 December 2025. Which is correct?

options.rationale: Three months relate to 2026 and must be carried forward.
Correct: 9 months belong to 2025 and 3 months to 2026.
The months have been swapped.
Money paid in advance is a prepayment (asset), not an accrual.

explanation: 2,160 ÷ 12 = 180 a month. April–December 2025 = 9 months = 1,620; January–March 2026 = 540 prepaid.

stem: The allowance for irrecoverable debts falls from US\$620 to US\$500. How is this shown in the income statement?

options.rationale: An expense arises only when the allowance increases.
Only the change appears in the income statement.

options.content: Nothing; the allowance appears only in the statement of financial position
options.rationale: The change in the allowance always passes through the income statement.
Correct: a decrease in the allowance increases profit.

explanation: A decrease in the allowance of 620 − 500 = 120 is added to gross profit as other income.

stem: A prepaid expense is deducted from the expense in the income statement and shown as a current asset.
explanation: True. It is an other receivable: the business has paid for a service it has not yet used.

stem: Depreciation for the year is deducted from the cash balance in the statement of financial position.
explanation: False. Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it is added to accumulated depreciation and deducted from the cost of the asset.

stem: Match each adjustment with its effect in the statement of financial position.
explanation: Accruals are other payables; prepayments other receivables; the allowance reduces receivables; depreciation builds up the provision; goods taken are drawings.
hints: Each adjustment also has an effect in the income statement; here match only the statement of financial position.

stem: Tatenda's draft profit, before any year-end adjustments, was US\$14,650. Adjustments: electricity owing US\$520; rates prepaid US\$360; depreciation US\$2,400; increase in the allowance for irrecoverable debts US\$90. Calculate the adjusted profit for the year.
explanation: 14,650 − 520 + 360 − 2,400 − 90 = 12,000. Reversing the accrual and prepayment gives 12,320.
workedSolution: 1. 14,650 − 520 + 360 − 2,400 − 90 = 12,000. Reversing the accrual and prepayment gives 12,320.
hints: Accruals and expenses reduce profit; prepayments increase it.

stem: Commission received in the trial balance is US\$1,150. A further US\$230 of commission for December 2025 had not yet been received. Calculate the commission received shown in the income statement for 2025.
explanation: Income due is added: 1,150 + 230 = 1,380. It is also a current asset (other receivable).
workedSolution: 1. Income due is added: 1,150 + 230 = 1,380. It is also a current asset (other receivable).

stem: After adjustments, a business has: inventory US\$8,350; trade receivables less allowance US\$6,120; prepaid rent US\$420; bank US\$1,990; cash US\$175; trade payables US\$5,480; accrued wages US\$660. Calculate the working capital.
explanation: Current assets 17,055 − current liabilities 6,140 = 10,915. Forgetting the accrued wages gives 11,575.
workedSolution: 1. Current assets 17,055 − current liabilities 6,140 = 10,915. Forgetting the accrued wages gives 11,575.
hints: Prepayments are current assets; accruals are current liabilities.

stem: Explain why the closing inventory, accruals and prepayments must be shown in **both** financial statements.

points.description: Each adjustment changes an income or expense figure (matching), affecting profit
and leaves an asset or liability at the year end, so the statement of financial position must show it to balance (double entry)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Adjustments match income and expenses to the year, changing profit; the other half of each entry is an asset or liability still held or owed at the year end, so it must appear in the statement of financial position, otherwise it would not balance.

explanation: Every adjustment is a double entry with one side in each statement.
hints: Think of the double entry behind each adjustment.

stem: Farai wants to reduce his allowance for irrecoverable debts from 5% to 1% of trade receivables "to show a better profit for the bank". Advise him.

points.description: Reducing the allowance would raise profit (the decrease is other income)
but would break the prudence concept / overstate receivables if debts are still doubtful
Advice: the allowance should be a realistic estimate based on past experience; misleading the bank is unethical

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lowering the allowance would increase profit, but if as many customers are still likely to default, receivables and profit would be overstated, breaking the prudence concept. He should keep a realistic allowance; showing the bank a misleading profit is unethical and could lead to a loan he cannot repay.

explanation: Profit must not be inflated by an unrealistic estimate.
hints: Which concept guides the size of the allowance?

stem:
Nyasha Dube's draft net profit for the year ended 31 December 2025 was US\$17,420. Her accountant then found:

| No. | Item |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Closing inventory was overvalued by US\$650 |
| 2 | Rates prepaid of US\$420 were treated as an expense of the year |
| 3 | Depreciation of US\$1,250 on fixtures was omitted |
| 4 | Commission receivable of US\$360 was not recorded |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which item **reduces** the net profit by the largest amount when it is corrected?

options.rationale: Reducing closing inventory lowers profit, but only by 650.
Removing a prepaid amount from the expense raises profit.
Recording income due raises profit.
Correct: the omitted depreciation of 1,250 is an extra expense.

parts.explanation: Items 1 and 3 reduce profit (by 650 and 1,250); items 2 and 4 increase it.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Complete the effect of each correction on the statement of financial position.

payload.template: Item 1: current assets {{blank:a}} by US\$650. Item 2: current assets {{blank:b}} by US\$420. Item 4: current assets {{blank:c}} by US\$360.

parts.explanation: Inventory falls; a prepayment and income due are new current assets.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State the effect of item 3 on the statement of financial position.

points.description: Provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) on fixtures increases by 1,250
so the net book value of non-current assets / capital (through lower profit) falls by 1,250

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The provision for depreciation on fixtures rises by 1,250, reducing their net book value by 1,250; closing capital falls by the same amount through the lower profit.

parts.explanation: Depreciation reduces both NBV and profit.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Name the concept that requires items 2 and 4 to be adjusted, and explain it briefly.

points.description: Income and expenses are recorded in the period they relate to, not when cash is paid or received

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The matching (accruals) concept: income and expenses belong to the year in which they are earned or incurred, whatever the date of payment.

parts.explanation: Prepayments and income due follow matching.

hints: For each item ask: does profit go up or down, and by how much?
